title: Skull Anatomy
descriptor: Cranial & Facial Bones, Sutures, Cranial Floor, Jaw Joint & Head Injuries
intro: The skull is formed by 22 bones in two groups, the brain case and the face. The brain case houses and shields the brain, while the facial bones give the face its structure and form the upper and lower jaws. Only the mandible, or lower jaw, is movable; the other bones are held together by immobile fibrous joints called sutures. The 3D model shows each bone separately and also includes the hyoid bone, which is not part of the skull.

keyFacts.label: Cranial floor
keyFacts.value: Anterior, middle and posterior cranial fossae; the foramen magnum lies in the posterior fossa

sections.heading: Brain case and facial bones
sections.body: The skull has two regions: the neurocranium, or brain case, which houses the brain, and the viscerocranium, which forms the face. The brain case is made up of eight bones: the paired parietal and temporal bones and the single frontal, occipital, sphenoid and ethmoid bones. The face has fourteen bones: the paired maxilla, palatine, zygomatic, nasal and lacrimal bones and inferior nasal conchae, and the single vomer and mandible. The ethmoid is counted among the cranial bones but also contributes to the structures of the face. The hyoid bone is an independent bone that does not contact any other bone, so it is not counted as part of the skull.

sections.heading: Sutures
sections.body: Sutures are fibrous joints in which connective tissue binds adjacent skull bones together. The coronal suture runs from side to side across the skull and joins the frontal bone to the right and left parietal bones. The sagittal suture runs along the midline of the skull, where the two parietal bones meet, and ends at the lambdoid suture. The lambdoid suture lies at the back of the skull, where the occipital bone meets the parietal bones. The squamous suture, on the side of the skull, joins the squamous part of the temporal bone to the parietal bone. Skull sutures are classed as synarthroses, although a few may allow slight movement between cranial bones.

sections.heading: Mandible and jaw joint
sections.body: The mandible, or lower jaw, is the only movable bone of the skull. Each side has a horizontal body and a vertical ramus, and the outer margin where they join is the angle. The flattened coronoid process on the ramus gives attachment to one of the biting muscles, while the condylar process is topped by the oval condyle. The condyle meets the mandibular fossa and articular tubercle of the temporal bone at the temporomandibular joint, where an articular disc lies between the bones. Gliding and hinge movements at this joint lower and raise the jaw, move it forwards and backwards, and shift it from side to side. A major chewing muscle that raises the mandible arises from the zygomatic arch, which is formed by the zygomatic and temporal bones.

sections.heading: Cranial floor and openings
sections.body: The floor of the cranial cavity forms three fossae that become deeper from front to back. The anterior fossa is the shallowest, and the lesser wings of the sphenoid form its back boundary. The middle fossa lies behind it, and its floor holds the optic canal, superior orbital fissure, foramen rotundum, foramen ovale and foramen spinosum. The posterior fossa is the deepest, extending to the occipital bone, and contains the foramen magnum, internal acoustic meatus, jugular foramina and hypoglossal canals. The skull base has many openings that pass nerves and blood vessels. The foramen magnum, the largest, is the passage by which the brain connects with the spinal cord, and the vertebral arteries also pass through it. The optic canal transmits the optic nerve and the ophthalmic artery.

sections.heading: Orbits, nose and sinuses
sections.body: Seven bones contribute to the walls of each orbit, which houses the eyeball and its muscles: the frontal, zygomatic, maxillary, palatine, ethmoid, lacrimal and sphenoid bones. The nasal septum divides the nasal cavity into halves; its upper part is the perpendicular plate of the ethmoid bone, its lower part is the vomer, and septal cartilage forms the front. The sinuses sit within several skull bones: the frontal sinus, above the eyebrows, is the most anterior; the maxillary sinuses, below the orbits, are the largest; and the sphenoid sinus, within the sphenoid body, is the most posterior. The ethmoid bone contains the ethmoid air cells, small air spaces between the orbit and the upper nasal cavity.

sections.heading: Growth and changes with age
sections.body: At birth the skull bones are not yet fused. The wide connective-tissue gaps between them, the fontanelles or soft spots, give the skull flexibility during birth, letting the bones move closer together or overlap slightly as the head passes through the birth canal. After birth they allow the skull to keep growing as the brain enlarges, and they decrease in size and close in early childhood. The cranial vault forms by intramembranous ossification, in which embryonic mesenchyme turns directly into bone, whereas the skull base forms by endochondral ossification. Late in life the sagittal, coronal and lambdoid sutures begin to ossify and fuse, a change called synostosis, meaning joined by bone.

sections.heading: Clinical relevance
sections.body: Most skull fractures heal by themselves, particularly simple linear fractures, although healing can take many months. At the pterion, where the frontal, parietal, temporal and sphenoid bones meet just above the ear, a blow to the side of the skull can tear the middle meningeal artery, a branch of the maxillary artery, and cause an epidural haematoma. Arterial bleeding into the epidural space accumulates quickly and does not cross suture lines. Temporomandibular joint disorder is a painful condition that can arise from arthritis, cartilage wear, muscle strain from overuse or teeth grinding, disc damage or a jaw injury. The NHS describes clicking, popping or grinding noises when the jaw moves as one of its features.

sections.heading: Head injuries and how they are assessed
sections.body: Most head injuries are not serious, but NHS advice lists signs that need urgent medical help, including a dent in the head, a head wound with something inside it, and fluid leaking from the ears or nose. In hospital, a CT scan is used to judge how serious a severe head injury is, because it shows whether there is any bleeding, bruising or swelling in the brain. Plain skull X-rays are no longer carried out for this purpose, because they give little information about brain damage.
